title: Determining Sample Size in Qualitative Research Across Case Study, Phenomenology, Grounded Theory, Narrative Inquiry and Ethnography: A Systematic Review
content: Introduction: Sample-size determination in qualitative research remains contested because adequacy is shaped by the research question, methodological purpose, participant specificity, data richness, analytical strategy and stopping rationale. The supplied literature reports numerical ranges, but does not establish universal minimums across qualitative methodologies. Methods: The researcher-selected databases and information sources were Google Scholar, ERIC. The eligibility protocol restricted publication years to 2025–2026. The exact calendar date of search execution was not recorded in the verified identification provenance; this is distinct from the publication-year eligibility range. A systematic review searched Google Scholar and ERIC using a prespecified Boolean strategy and publication eligibility range of 2025–2026. Results: Across the synthesis, sample adequacy was primarily treated as a design-sensitive judgement rather than a universal numerical threshold. Focused, homogeneous and information-rich samples generally supported smaller samples, whereas broad, comparative and heterogeneous designs required more data. Saturation was useful when operationalised as an ongoing evaluative process, but its meaning and applicability were contested. Grounded Theory provided the clearest method-specific stopping logic through theoretical sampling and theoretical saturation. Ethnographic guidance was comparatively underdeveloped, while numerical ranges for phenomenology and narrative inquiry remained illustrative rather than definitive. Discussion/Conclusion: While there was no generally accepted minimum sample size was established for any reviewed methodology, there seem to be a recommendation of 10 to 15 interviews. Furthermore, a defensible sample-size decision should be justified prospectively in relation to design, scope, sampling logic, information power, data quality, analytic aims and an explicitly documented stopping assessment.
